transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. Smith, I’m here because... for months now, I’ve been seeing the exact same pattern. My sister’s appointments keep getting moved around, her bills show up completely wrong, and people just conveniently 'forget' to call me back. 

It’s funny because at my job—I supervise the administrative support team at a regional office—if one of my clerks 'forgot' to return an important call, I’d have them written up. Just last week, I had a new temp, Brenda, who couldn't even transfer a call properly. I had to sit there for forty-five minutes explaining a basic multi-line phone system to a woman with a bachelor's degree. She had this awful floral perfume on, too, gave me a terrible headache the whole afternoon. 

But anyway, what I'm saying is, even when everyone tells me it’s just 'clerical mistakes' with my sister's stuff, I know better. I run an office, I know how these things actually work. I know they’re keeping information from me on purpose. They are actively trying to push me out of all the decisions regarding her. It’s just like my neighbor when he put up that new privacy fence without even checking the property line or talking to the HOA... people just scheme behind your back and expect you not to notice. So, yes, that's why I'm here.

Aside from what's happening with your sister's care right now, have you generally felt throughout your life—going back to your teens or twenties—that other people, like coworkers, friends, or family, are often trying to deceive or take advantage of you?

No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, back in my twenties, things were perfectly fine. I had a great group of friends when I was getting my bachelor's degree. My roommate, Linda, we trusted each other with everything. We used to share a car, this beat-up blue Honda Civic. The heater in that thing was completely broken, which was miserable in the winter. 

Speaking of winter, they still haven't plowed the visitor parking at my complex, and it's been three days since it snowed. I had to call the property management company twice yesterday. The girl who answered—another one who clearly doesn't know how to take a message—sounded like she was chewing gum right into the headset. It is so unprofessional. I always tell my clerks, 'If I hear you chewing on a call, you're going home.' It just sets a terrible tone for the whole organization, you know? It's about basic respect. 

But, um... wait, what was the question? Oh, about people deceiving me my whole life. No, no, it's just this current situation with my sister. I never had these kinds of issues with people scheming against me when I was younger. This is entirely different.

When you think about your sister's mixed-up appointments and bills, is there any part of you that considers it might just be an honest mistake or miscommunication, or are you completely certain it's intentional?

Honest mistake? No, absolutely not. Like I was saying, it has been going on for months. The appointments constantly getting moved, the bills showing up completely wrong, the unreturned phone calls... everyone keeps telling me it's just clerical errors, but I am completely certain it's intentional. I know they are keeping information from me on purpose to push me out of the decisions about her care. 

I know an honest mistake when I see one. Like on Tuesday, I went to pick up my dry cleaning, and the girl at the counter handed me a pair of wool slacks that belonged to a man named Arthur. Now, that is an honest mistake. She just misread the ticket. Although, honestly, they really should train their staff better on the tagging system over there. We used a color-coded filing system at my first supervisory job back in the nineties, and it worked flawlessly. We never lost a single document. My boss at the time, Mr. Henderson, he was a real stickler for organization. He used to bring in these amazing blueberry muffins on Fridays from this little bakery downtown that closed years ago... they had those big sugar crystals on top, you know the kind? I haven't had a muffin like that in ages. 

But anyway... yes, to answer your question, I am absolutely certain they're doing it to my sister on purpose. It's not a mistake.

Would you say that, in general, you tend to hold yourself and others to very strict standards of order, correctness, and rule-following in most areas of your life—at work, at home, with finances—even when it causes friction with people around you?

Strict standards? Well, I suppose so, yes. I just believe things should be done correctly. If there's a rule or a procedure, it's there for a reason, right? Like at the office, I expect my clerks to follow the manual to the letter. It's not about being difficult, it's about efficiency. 

Speaking of efficiency, I was at the grocery store yesterday, and the cashier—this young kid, probably still in high school—was bagging my groceries so haphazardly. He put the raw chicken right on top of the fresh produce! I had to stop him and explain cross-contamination. He rolled his eyes at me, can you believe that? The lack of respect for basic hygiene is just astounding these days. It reminds me of this restaurant I went to last month, an Italian place. The waiter brought out my pasta, and I swear the plate was chipped. I sent it back, of course. You can't serve food on chipped china, it's a health hazard. They ended up comping my dessert, a tiramisu, which honestly was a bit soggy anyway. I make a much better tiramisu at home. The secret is to dip the ladyfingers very quickly, just a quick dunk in the espresso, otherwise, they get mushy. 

But, um, yes, I do like things done right. Whether it's at work or anywhere else, I just think if you're going to do something, you should do it properly.

If your sister's care team showed you documented proof—like time-stamped call logs or the original clerical records—that these errors were genuine mistakes and not intentional, do you think that evidence could change your mind, or would you still be certain they were done on purpose?

Documented proof? Like logs and records? No, absolutely not. I wouldn't believe it for a second. I mean, I'm here because for months now I've been seeing the exact same pattern. My sister's appointments get moved, the bills show up wrong, people conveniently 'forget' to call me back. And even when everyone, including the facility director, says it's just mistakes, I know they're keeping information from me and trying to push me out of decisions. You can't just fake a pattern like that. 

Well, actually, I suppose you *can* fake records. I remember back in 2008, I had this clerk, Sarah. Sweet girl, but completely disorganized. She was supposed to be logging the incoming mail, and I caught her backdating the entry stamps because she'd let a whole stack sit on her desk for three days. Three days! In a busy office, that is an eternity. We had to implement a whole new tracking system after that. I spent an entire weekend designing the new spreadsheet. I even color-coded the priority levels. My husband at the time—we're divorced now, he moved to Florida—he complained that I was working on a Sunday, but I told him, 'If you want things done right, you have to put in the time.' He never really understood my work ethic. He was more the type to just sit on the couch and watch golf all weekend. I never understood the appeal of golf. It's just walking around a big lawn, hitting a little ball. 

But anyway, no, a logbook wouldn't change my mind. I know what they're doing. They're trying to push me out, and a piece of paper isn't going to convince me otherwise.

Has this conviction that your sister's caregivers are deliberately deceiving you led you to take any specific actions—like filing a formal complaint, contacting a lawyer, or confronting staff directly—and if so, how have those situations turned out?

Well, I haven't called a lawyer yet, but I certainly have confronted the staff. I've had to. I mean, they are deliberately trying to keep me out of the loop. I've demanded meetings with the facility director, and honestly, those family meetings have become very tense. My brother was at the last one, and he just sat there, not saying a word, while I was trying to get straight answers out of them. He’s always been like that, though. Even when we were kids, if there was any kind of conflict, he would just disappear into his room and build those little model airplanes. He had hundreds of them hanging from his ceiling. I always wondered how my mother dusted them. She was meticulous about dusting. She used this lemon oil polish that smelled so strong, it would give me a headache if I stayed in the room too long. I still can't stand the smell of artificial lemon. 

But anyway, yes, it's caused some tension. And it's not just with my sister's care team. It's... well, it's spilling over a bit at work, too. I've had a few uncomfortable conversations lately because I've been pressing people harder about routine mistakes than I used to. I just have zero tolerance for it right now. If a clerk misfiles a report, I need to know exactly *why* it happened, not just that it was an accident. I'm still managing all my responsibilities, of course—I run a tight ship—but I can tell it has started to affect how people respond to me. They get very defensive. 

People are just so defensive these days. You can't even offer constructive criticism without someone taking it personally. Like that cashier at the grocery store I mentioned. I was just trying to help him avoid giving someone salmonella! But nobody wants to listen to experience anymore. They all think they know best because they can look something up on their phones in two seconds. I miss the days when people actually respected authority and took pride in their work.

Outside of your sister's care team, do you currently believe that specific people elsewhere in your life—like coworkers or neighbors—are also deliberately deceiving or scheming against you, or is this feeling of being deliberately deceived limited only to the situation with your sister?

Scheming? Oh, no, heavens no. It’s strictly the people at my sister's facility. Outside of dealing with her appointments and trying to get straight answers out of that care team, everything else is perfectly normal. I still keep my home in absolute order, I pay my bills on time, and I do my job just like I always have. 

Actually, speaking of paying bills, I had to go down to the post office yesterday to mail my property tax check because the county's online portal was down again. The line was practically out the door. There was this woman in front of me with three toddlers, and she was trying to mail a massive, oddly-shaped box to Germany. Who mails a package to Germany on a Tuesday at lunchtime? It took twenty minutes. I just don't understand why people don't use the self-service kiosk for things like that. It's right there in the lobby! I read an article recently about how the postal service is hemorrhaging money, and honestly, if that's how they manage the midday rush, I am not surprised in the least. My uncle Arthur used to be a postman back in the seventies, back when they actually walked the routes and knew everyone's names. He got this terrible dog bite once on his calf from a Golden Retriever. People think Golden Retrievers are so friendly, but they can be very territorial. He had to get six stitches. 

But, um, what was I saying? Right, my neighbors and coworkers. No, they aren't doing anything to me. People at work or in my family might think I’m a bit too focused on this situation with my sister, but I assure you, I’m not falling apart or acting strangely in other parts of my life. I'm just dealing with a very specific problem that needs to be fixed.

Setting aside any actual proof, is there any part of you—even a small part—that wonders if your certainty about this being intentional might be a bit stronger than the situation calls for, or does that possibility not make sense to you at all?

No, that possibility doesn't make sense to me at all. Why would I doubt myself when the evidence is right there? Like I said before, I’m here because for months now I’ve been seeing the exact same pattern. My sister’s appointments get moved, the bills show up wrong, and people just conveniently 'forget' to call me back. And even when everyone keeps telling me it’s just innocent mistakes, I know they’re keeping information from me and trying to push me out of decisions. 

You know, people pushing you out... it actually reminds me of this regional manager I had back in the nineties, Mr. Abernathy. He was always trying to sideline the experienced supervisors so he could bring in his own people. He was a very slick talker. He had this awful comb-over, though, and he drove a maroon Buick LeSabre. I always thought maroon was such a dreary color for a car. My first car was a bright yellow Datsun. Oh, I loved that little car. The heater was practically useless, so in the winter I had to wear my heavy wool peacoat just to drive to work. Wool coats are so heavy, aren't they? They just drag down your shoulders. I finally bought one of those lightweight down puffer coats last year on sale at Macy's. It is so much more comfortable, especially when you're carrying groceries. The plastic bags they use at the store now are so flimsy, they cut right into your hands if you don't have good pockets to rest them on. 

But... I'm sorry, what did you ask me? Right, if I'm too certain. No, I'm not overreacting. I'm just observant. I know exactly what they're doing with my sister's care, and I won't let them get away with it.

Doctor: Have you ever felt that the staff might be acting maliciously because of something specific you did or said, or do you think they are doing this for some other reason?

Patient: Oh, no, it's not because of anything I did. I've been perfectly reasonable. I think they just want to avoid accountability, and I'm the only one holding their feet to the fire. They want to cut corners and not have anyone checking their work. 

Speaking of checking work, I had to completely redo the quarterly supply inventory at the office last week because my new assistant, Brenda, just guessed at the numbers instead of actually counting the toner cartridges. She’s very sweet, but she’s just not detail-oriented. She brought in these amazing homemade blueberry muffins on Tuesday, though. The tops were perfectly crusty with that coarse sugar on them. I haven't baked muffins in years. I used to have this heavy cast-iron muffin pan that belonged to my grandmother. It weighed an absolute ton, but it baked everything so evenly. I think I gave it to my niece when she moved into her first apartment. She moved to Chicago, right near the lake. The wind coming off that lake in January is just brutal. I visited her once and my ears ached for three days afterwards. I told her she needs to invest in a really good, heavy wool hat, not those flimsy acrylic ones you buy at the drugstore. 

But no, it's not personal against me. They just don't like that I'm paying attention.

I'm not entirely sure what you mean by that. I haven't really noticed anything like that happening, if that's what you're asking. I just try to keep my eyes open and notice what's actually going on right in front of me. 

Speaking of noticing things, I've been trying to pay more attention to the birds in my backyard lately. I bought this gorgeous copper bird feeder on clearance at a garden center in the next town over. I had to take Route 9 to get there, and let me tell you, the potholes are just horrendous this time of year. The city council keeps promising they'll fix them, but they just slap down that cheap patch material that washes away in the very first spring rain. We had a terrible rainstorm last April that actually flooded my basement with two inches of water. I had to throw out three boxes of old tax returns. Not that you need to keep them for more than seven years anyway. I always tell my clerks at the office, you only need to keep the files for seven years and then they go straight to the cross-cut shredder. We have this massive industrial shredder in the copy room, and it's so loud you can barely hear yourself think when Brenda is running the monthly purges. She always does it right before lunch, too, which drives me absolutely up the wall because I’m trying to finish my morning reports. 

Oh, dear, I’m rambling again, aren't I? I'm sorry, what were we just talking about? You asked me something and I completely lost my train of thought.

Doctor: Have you ever felt that they are doing this to test your loyalty or to see how far you'll go to protect your sister, or is it purely about them wanting to cut corners?

Patient: Test my loyalty? No, I don't think it's a test. Like I said, it's just about them trying to hide their mistakes and cut corners. I've always been very loyal to my sister, I don't need anyone to test that. 

Speaking of loyalty, we had this administrative assistant at the office years ago, Cheryl. She was fiercely loyal to the company, worked there for almost thirty years. She even kept a framed picture of the founder on her desk, right next to her collection of ceramic frogs. She had dozens of those little frogs. Some of them were quite valuable, I think. She bought a lot of them at antique shows on the weekends. I went to an antique show once, in this huge drafty barn out in the country. It smelled like old books and dust. I ended up buying this beautiful vintage globe, the kind with the raised relief for the mountains. It's sitting in my living room right now, right next to my favorite armchair. It's a wingback chair, upholstered in this lovely floral chintz. It’s so comfortable to read in. I’ve been trying to read more historical biographies lately. I just finished one about Eleanor Roosevelt. She had such a fascinating life, didn't she? All that traveling she did. 

Wait, what did you ask me? Something about testing my loyalty? No, no, they aren't testing me. They just want to do less work and not get caught.

Doctor: You mentioned earlier that the staff might be trying to avoid accountability. Have you ever felt that they are doing this to intentionally cause harm to you or your sister, or is it just about them trying to hide their mistakes?

Patient: Oh, no, not intentionally causing harm. I don't think they're sitting around plotting against us like some sort of cartoon villains. It's really just laziness, you know? They just want to sweep their mistakes under the rug. 

Speaking of sweeping, I had to buy a new broom last week because the bristles on my old one were completely bent out of shape. I found this really nice one with angled bristles at the hardware store downtown. The hardware store is right next to this little bakery that sells the most incredible sourdough bread. The crust is so thick and chewy. I always try to get there early on Saturday mornings before they sell out. Last Saturday, I was in line behind this woman who had a tiny little Yorkshire Terrier in her purse. It was wearing a tiny knitted sweater, if you can believe it. A bright yellow sweater with a little blue anchor on it. It reminded me of a sweater my sister had when we were kids. She loved that sweater so much she wore it until the elbows completely gave out. My mother tried to patch it, but she was never very good at sewing. She preferred knitting. She knitted me this massive, heavy afghan when I went off to college. It was so warm, but the colors were just atrocious—mustard yellow and avocado green. Very seventies. I think it's still folded up in the cedar chest at the foot of my bed. 

But no, to answer your question, they aren't trying to hurt us. They're just lazy and don't want anyone checking their work.

Doctor: I see. It sounds like you feel they're just being careless. Have you noticed any other groups or individuals, besides the staff, acting strangely or trying to cover things up?

Patient: Other groups? No, no, I haven't noticed anything like that. Just the staff at that facility, really. I don't pay much attention to other people's business unless it directly affects me or my sister. 

Though, speaking of covering things up, you should see the way the landscapers try to hide the bald spots on my front lawn. They just throw down a handful of that cheap green dyed mulch and think I won't notice. I pay good money for a professional lawn service, and they treat my yard like an afterthought. I had to call their manager last Tuesday, right in the middle of my favorite cooking show. I was watching this wonderful woman make a classic French bouillabaisse. The way she handled the seafood was just masterful. It made me want to go down to the fish market by the pier. I haven't been down there since my sister and I took that day trip three summers ago. We bought fresh scallops and ate them right out of the paper container while watching the seagulls fight over french fries. One of those gulls was huge, absolute monster of a bird, and it swooped down and practically snatched a fry right out of a little boy's hand. The mother screamed so loud I thought someone had been shot. It was quite a commotion. We ended up leaving early because the wind picked up and it got terribly chilly. I always tell people to bring a light cardigan when they go near the water, even in July. You just never know when the sea breeze is going to turn on you. 

Anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right. No, I haven't noticed anyone else acting strangely. Just the staff cutting corners with my sister's care.

Doctor: That sounds like a frustrating experience with the landscapers. Given what you've noticed with the staff at the facility, do you ever feel like they are trying to communicate with each other in a secret way, maybe using codes or signals when you're around?

Patient: Secret codes? No, no, they aren't smart enough for that. They just whisper sometimes when they think I'm not listening, or they'll give each other these little looks, you know? Like, 'Oh, here she comes again.' But no codes or anything out of a spy movie. 

I did read a spy novel recently, though. It was about this woman in World War II who worked in a code-breaking unit. Bletchley Park, I think it was called. Fascinating stuff, really. They used these massive, clunky machines to decipher messages. It made me think about how much technology has changed. My niece, she's in her twenties, she can type faster on her little phone with just her thumbs than I ever could on my old Smith Corona typewriter. I loved that typewriter. It was this beautiful seafoam green color. I used to type up all the meeting minutes for the neighborhood watch committee back in the nineties. We were very organized back then. We even had these little laminated badges we wore when we went on patrol. Not that anything ever happened in our neighborhood. The most exciting thing was when Mrs. Gable's tabby cat got stuck in the old oak tree at the end of the cul-de-sac. The fire department actually had to come get him down. The fireman who climbed the ladder was so handsome, he looked just like a young Robert Redford. Mrs. Gable practically swooned. She baked them two dozen snickerdoodle cookies the next day as a thank you. I've never been able to get my snickerdoodles right. They always turn out too flat. I think my baking soda might be expired. 

Anyway, no, I haven't seen them using any secret signals. They just try to avoid me when they can.

Doctor: It's good to know they aren't using codes. You mentioned they whisper and give each other looks. Have you ever felt like you have a special ability to understand what they are thinking or feeling, even without them saying it out loud?

Patient: A special ability? Oh, like reading minds? Heavens, no. I'm just observant, that's all. Anyone paying attention could tell they're just annoyed I'm checking up on them. 

Though, sometimes I wish I could read minds, especially when I'm trying to figure out what my brother-in-law wants for his birthday. The man is impossible to shop for. Last year, I got him this beautiful set of whiskey glasses, the heavy crystal kind, and he just left them sitting in the box in the garage. I saw them when I went over there to drop off some tomato plants. I grow my own tomatoes, you know. Big, juicy heirlooms. The secret is crushing up eggshells into the soil for the calcium. My grandmother taught me that. She had a garden the size of a football field, or at least it felt like it when I was little. We used to spend hours out there pulling weeds. She wore this enormous straw hat with a faded pink ribbon that would flap in the wind. She got it at a state fair back in the fifties. I haven't been to a state fair in ages. The last time I went, I ate a deep-fried candy bar and thought my stomach was going to stage a rebellion. It was so greasy, but somehow absolutely delicious at the same time. You really shouldn't eat things like that, though, not at my age. I've been trying to stick to a Mediterranean diet lately. Lots of olive oil and fish. It's supposed to be good for your heart. 

But no, I definitely can't read their minds. I just know what guilt looks like when I see it.

Thinking back to your twenties and thirties, before any of this trouble with your sister's care began, would you say you were already someone who insisted on strict rules, perfect order, and doing things 'the right way' at work and at home, even when it caused friction with people back then?

Strict rules? Perfect order? Well, I don't know if I'd say I was strict, but I did like things done properly. I was an office manager for a real estate firm back then, and you have to keep things organized when you're dealing with all those contracts and escrow accounts. It's just common sense. 

Speaking of real estate, the market right now is just absolutely wild, isn't it? The house two doors down from me, the one with the horrible yellow siding, just sold for over asking price in three days. Three days! And the people who bought it, this young couple, they immediately started tearing up the front yard to put in some kind of drought-resistant rock garden. It looks like a quarry, honestly. I don't understand this new trend of getting rid of grass. When I was growing up, a nice green lawn was a point of pride. My father used to be out there every Saturday morning with the edger, making sure the lines along the sidewalk were perfectly straight. He had this old push mower that he refused to replace, even when the motorized ones became popular. He said it built character to push it yourself. He was always talking about building character. He made my brother and me wash his car every Sunday before church. A big, boat of a thing, a 1972 Buick LeSabre. We had to use these special chamois cloths to dry it so there wouldn't be water spots. I can still smell the turtle wax we used. It smelled a bit like coconut, which always made me crave those little coconut macaroon cookies they sell at the bakery downtown. The bakery is still there, actually, run by the grandson of the original owner. He doesn't make the macaroons quite as well as his grandfather did, though. They're always a bit too dry on the inside. 

But anyway, what was the question? Oh, friction with people. No, I wouldn't say I caused friction. I just expected people to do their jobs correctly. Just like I expect the staff at the facility to do theirs.
